item.title: Türkiye climate summit’s finance gap threatens its promise of action
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Activism, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Change Mitigation, Environment, Fossil Fuels, and Industry
item.description:
- Discussions and announcements in the first week of the annual UN climate summit in Antalya have exposed the gap between ambitious climate promises and the money needed to put them into practice.
- New initiatives proposed by hosts Türkiye and Australia may help countries prepare projects, but they cannot replace the predictable public finance that developing nations and emerging economies need.
- As negotiations enter their second and final week, disagreements over finance and the transition away from fossil fuels threaten to derail the summit’s promise of action.
item.content:encoded: Halfway through the annual United Nations climate summit being held in Türkiye’s Antalya, nearly 200 governments face the familiar question of where is the money to turn their promises into action? The meeting was billed as a turning point, a chance to move beyond pledges and start delivering results. However, as ministers prepare to take over negotiations in the second week, the central obstacle that has frustrated climate talks for years remains unresolved. Developing countries need far more money to protect their people from climate change and shift to cleaner energy. Developed countries have yet to agree on how much they will provide, in what form and when. UN Secretary-General António Guterres captured the scale of the crisis at the leaders’ summit on November 11. “The brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us,” he said. Global emissions reached a record in 2025, and the world is certain to exceed the 1.5°C warming limit set out by the legally binding Paris Agreement in 2015. But the scale and duration of that overshoot can still be limited through faster action, Guterres said. That action will cost money. It means cleaner electricity, safer roads and buildings, better water systems, protection for farms and coastal communities, and early warnings that can save lives. Yet the countries most exposed to climate impacts often have the least money to prepare for them. The first week in Antalya has produced new initiatives and political promises. It has not produced a breakthrough on finance. That…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Climate movement takes its fight beyond emissions at Türkiye summit
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Activism, Cities and Towns, Climate Change, Environment, Forests, Fossil Fuels, Indigenous Rights, Pollution, and United Nations
item.description:
- Thousands of activists, workers and indigenous groups took to Antalya’s streets, turning a rainy day into a vibrant demonstration for climate justice during the ongoing climate conference.
- The protesters challenged fossil fuel dependence, corporate control of natural resources, forest destruction and the growing inequalities of climate change.
- Their demands went beyond emissions cuts to call for public control of energy, workers’ rights, climate finance and accountability for polluters.
item.content:encoded: A grey, rain-soaked day in Antalya in Türkiye burst into a riot of colour, music and slogans on November 14, when civil society called for a global day of action, held alongside COP31, the ongoing UN climate conference. Bright flags, hand-painted banners, giant street installations and costumed performers filled the city centre as thousands of climate activists, trade unionists and civil society campaigners marched through the streets. The rain did little to dampen their enthusiasm. Chants rang out against fossil fuels, corporate greed, forest destruction and economic injustice. The procession offered a striking contrast to the air-conditioned and sterile negotiating rooms of the international climate talks taking place in the city. Inside, government representatives were engaged in painstaking negotiations over finance, emissions and national commitments. Outside, people from different countries and movements were making their demands heard in a more direct and colourful manner. Their message was that climate change cannot be addressed simply by reducing emissions. It also requires confronting the economic interests and political choices that drive environmental destruction and inequality. The march opened the People’s Climate Summit, a parallel gathering held from November 14 to 18. More than 130 organisations are to be involved in around 150 events, with participants from 34 countries, according to its organisers. The procession on November 14 brought together movements working on issues ranging from fossil fuels and forest protection to workers’ rights, food systems, gender equality and peace. item.title: Three years on, Teesta’s flood survivors live in limbo as the river creeps closer
item.dc:creator: Yalember Dewan
item.author: Simrinsirur
item.reporting-project: Climate Connections and The India Water Story
item.topic-tags: Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Dams, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Floods, Glacial Lake Outburst Flood, Glaciers, Himalayas, Human Rights, Impacts of Climate Change, Land Rights, and Rivers
item.description:
- Nearly three years after the October 2023 glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) on Teesta river, displaced families still live in makeshift relief camps in Kalimpong, West Bengal, while those whose homes survived face a river that now sits closer and floods again each monsoon.
- Residents say there was no working early-warning system the night of the flood, and repeated surveys of damage have yet to produce housing, with 116 planned houses still awaiting state finance sanction.
- Sikkim sanctioned 4,100 houses and rental aid for those affected by the GLOF, but West Bengal never declared the flood a disaster and offered no housing scheme, leaving survivors in fear of eviction.
item.content:encoded: “When the flood took everything from me, it took more than my home and livelihood, it took away the place I once had in society. People look at us differently now. The relationships and respect we once had are no longer the same. I am not a beggar, and I was never born into a life like this.” Bijay Pradhan, 36, speaks about a loss that goes beyond a house. Before October 2023, when a Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) surged through the Teesta river, his family had a home of their own and relied partly on agriculture and livestock rearing. After the flood, he became a daily-wage labourer supporting his mother, wife and two children. The family now lives in a temporary relief camp in Teesta Bazaar in Kalimpong, West Bengal, alongside hundreds of others. For him, losing the house also meant losing independence and social standing. The 2023 GLOF was caused by a breach of the South Lhonak Lake in upstream Sikkim, impacting 80,000 people. A 2025 study published in Science estimated that 270 million cubic metres of sediment were swept downstream by the flood. In Kalimpong, the Teesta riverbed reportedly rose between six and 14 metres, a central government committee tasked with documenting the river’s changed morphology found. Nearly three years after the flood, people are still rebuilding their lives on unstable land, with the possibility of another flood lingering each monsoon. The region experienced consecutive flash floods in 2024 and 2025, exacerbating the landscape’s vulnerabilities. The…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Geopolitical shocks put energy security and clean energy transition in focus
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Carbon emissions, Carbon Finance, Cities and Towns, Clean Energy, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Coal, Energy, Environment, Environmental Economics, Fossil Fuels, Global Warming, Green Energy, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Industry, and Renewable Energy
item.description:
- Geopolitical shocks have made domestic clean energy a strategic necessity, but temporary falls in fossil fuel use will not deliver lasting emissions cuts.
- India must move beyond adding renewable capacity to displacing fossil fuels across its economy. Its ethanol programme shows how pursuing energy independence can create new pressures on land, water and food.
- Developing countries need affordable finance and technology to transition without bearing an unfair share of the costs.
item.content:encoded: The wars disrupting global energy markets have exposed the strategic weakness of an economy built on fossil fuels. Countries dependent on imported oil and gas can find their growth, public finances and energy supplies hostage to conflicts thousands of kilometres away. A threatened shipping route or an interruption in supplies can quickly raise the cost of transport, electricity and food. For India and much of the developing world, this is not an occasional inconvenience. It is a structural vulnerability. The case for domestic clean energy has never been stronger. Solar and wind power do not have to pass through contested shipping routes, and once installed, they provide electricity without the recurring cost of importing fuel. Electrifying transport and industry can reduce dependence on oil and gas. The transition is no longer simply an obligation born out of the climate crisis. It is now an economic and a strategic necessity. But there is a distinction that governments cannot afford to overlook. Energy security is not the same as a just transition. A country can reduce its dependence on imported fossil fuels while creating new dependencies on critical minerals, intensifying competition for farmland and water, or leaving consumers with unreliable and unaffordable power. Developing countries face the harder task of building clean energy systems while coping with high borrowing costs, limited access to technology and far fewer financial resources than wealthy economies. That is the choice confronting delegates at the United Nations climate summit COP31 in Türkiye. The energy crisis has made…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: No land to call their own, migrants and elephants coexist on a transient landscape
item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Biodiversity, Conservation, Elephants, Habitat Fragmentation, Himalayas, Human Wildlife Conflict, Land Rights, Mammals, Migration, Rivers, Villages, Water, and Wildlife
item.description:
- In a charland on the Teesta in West Bengal, the lives and livelihoods, shaped by a constantly shifting landscape, are increasingly threatened by climate change.
- Although charlands support agriculture and provide refuge to landless migrants, residents face insecure land rights and precarious livelihoods.
- Elephants are increasingly using cultivated charlands as feeding grounds, adding to the challenges faced by residents.
- Human-elephant coexistence depends on understanding the wider landscape, including changing river systems, fragmented forests and expanding agriculture.
item.content:encoded: Fifty-seven-year-old Budharu Muhammed recalls a time when bombs, shells and ammunition flowed down the Teesta towards Premganj char, a sandbar settlement around 15 km from Jalpaiguri town in West Bengal. It was 2023, when a massive glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) from South Lhonak Lake in the Sikkim Himalayas caused a major surge in the Teesta, damaging infrastructure and affecting hydropower projects downstream. Silt, sand and rubble were flushed downstream. According to Muhammed, some army camps were flooded, explaining the sudden appearance of military materiel in his village and the panic it triggered. “There were other toxic things flowing down from medical shops and factories, oil from vehicles and gas cylinders. The water was murky with a layer of oil on top,” he says. People complained of skin rashes and itching after coming into contact with the water, he recalls, describing a time of uncertainty and fear. Located under Paharpur Gram Panchayat in the Sadar block of Jalpaiguri district, Premganj char, also known as Jaliapara, is identified as a highly vulnerable charland in the district’s disaster management plans. Adding to the woes of residents facing constant flooding and erosion is another threat: the movement of maljurians, or groups of male elephants. Maljurians comprise younger males and experienced adults that explore new landscapes, largely in search of food, explains Avijan Saha, a researcher with the wildlife conservation non-profit Airavat Trust who has studied the landscape for over a decade. “Other elephants can then follow the routes they have explored. These groups…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Wildlife trade discourse overlooks trade in plants and other natural resources [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Lokesh MamThangsoi M. KhiamniunganUttara Mendiratta
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Commentary, Community based conservation, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Environmental Law, Forests, Insects, Plants, Wildlife Protection Act, Wildlife Trade, and Wildlife Trafficking
item.description:
- Wild plant trafficking remains largely overlooked, despite over 20% of assessed plant species being threatened with extinction.
- Unregulated trade extends beyond medicinal plants to orchids, mushrooms, insects and wildlife products, creating ecological and social consequences.
- Community-led monitoring and protection are crucial to conservation, alongside policies that recognise local livelihoods and support sustainable trade.
- The views in the commentary are that of the authors.
item.content:encoded: A simple question during a panel discussion on illegal wildlife trade at the Indian Wildlife Ecology Conference (IWEC) in 2024 got us thinking: What about plants and its trade? The panel admitted to the prevailing problem of “plant blindness”. While illegal wildlife trade brings to mind trafficking of orangutans, parrots, elephant ivory, and other endangered wildlife, there is rarely any conversation around plants. Except for the trade in high-value timber and ornamental plants, which have received some attention in the public eye, the trade in plants goes on largely unacknowledged. Over 20% of all plant species assessed by the IUCN Red List are threatened with extinction — a comparable level of extinction risk to mammals. And like the trade in wild animals, the trade in wild plants has serious and urgent conservation implications for species and ecosystems. Many researchers have highlighted the problem of large-scale extraction of threatened medicinal plants, which are often illegally laundered into legal markets. The collection happens across wide geographical expanses and involves local residents. The legal and conservation implications of this collection are not often apparent to local residents, nor is this considered a priority for enforcement agencies. As a result, the trade goes on, underreported and unaddressed. For many species, researchers acknowledge that local extinctions could happen without being recorded. A forest in Nagaland. While the topic of illegal wildlife trade brings to mind many endangered mammals, there is rarely any conversation around plants. Representative image by Mike Prince via Flickr (CC BY 2.0).…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.author: Priyanka Shankar

item.content:encoded: A recent study of Kerala’s Vypin-Kadamakkudy barrier island system recorded 20,927 dung beetles from 29 species, far more diversity than researchers expected in such an urbanising landscape. Dung beetles are scarab beetles, mostly of the subfamily Scarabaeinae, that feed, breed and nest in animal dung. Encased in a hard exoskeleton, they are also remarkably strong. The male horned dung beetle (Onthophagus taurus), for example, can pull up to 1,141 times its own body weight; equivalent to an average human adult lifting six double-decker buses. Dung beetles occur in forests, grasslands and deserts on every continent except Antarctica. They are vital ecological engineers, as they recycle animal waste, which in turn helps reduce methane emissions, aerate soil, and suppress pest flies. They are also secondary seed dispersers. There are more than 6,000 species of dung beetles worldwide, of which about 400-500 have been recorded in India. They are grouped by how they handle dung — rollers, such as Gymnopleurus species, shape it into balls and roll them away to bury elsewhere; tunnellers, such as Onitis species, dig chambers beneath the pat and bury it; and dwellers, such as Oniticellus species, breed inside the pat itself. They also differ in what they eat. Some species are generalists, surviving on the dung of any animal, while others are specialists, such as Heliocopris dominus, which can survive only on wild elephant dung. Most Indian dung beetles have not yet been assessed on the IUCN Red List. Researchers say that habitat loss and fragmentation are…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Open genetic data and unclear rules keep biodiversity fund largely empty
item.dc:creator: Kundan Pandey
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity
item.description:
- COP17 in Yerevan deferred the Cali Fund’s key rules to 2028, leaving the fund with a meagre sum from five small companies.
- Disagreements over certificates that companies want, unsettled payment rules and untraceable genetic data in open databases slow the fund’s progress.
- Experts are divided on the fix, while communities that protect biodiversity have yet to receive any funds.
item.content:encoded: A decade after countries first agreed to discuss the issue, the sharing of benefits from digital sequence information (DSI), the genetic data of plants, animals and microbes stored in online databases, has made little progress. This is despite a fund set up under the United Nations in 2024, which seeks to make corporations share part of their profits of benefiting from using genetic data from nature. COP17, the UN biodiversity summit that ended on October 31 in Yerevan, Armenia, was expected to settle how the fund would work. Instead, countries deferred the key decisions to the next summit, COP18 in 2028. The Cali Fund, named after the Colombian city where it was agreed, was expected to raise around $1 billion a year. As of November 10, 2026, it had received $10,588. At COP17, countries were expected to settle a few questions left over from the previous summit in Cali. For example, which companies should pay, and how much? Should payments be linked to how much DSI a company uses? How can the online databases that hold DSI be made accountable to all countries? And how should the money be shared among countries and communities? “Unfortunately, the preparations between the two COPs did not reach a point where COP17 could take a final call on them with proper information,” said Nithin Ramakrishnan, a senior researcher at the Third World Network (TWN). “So, they all relied on interim measures, and the goalpost has now shifted to COP18.” “Much of the two years…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Communities experiment with new ways to protect old caves
item.dc:creator: Jyoti ThakurPratik Chakarborty
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Climate Change, Community based conservation, Environment, Indigenous Peoples, Tourism, and Tribes
item.description:
- Meghalaya’s caves preserve a remarkable record of the planet’s climate history, including evidence of the 4,200-year-old climate event that marks the beginning of the Meghalayan Age.
- Climate change and mining are threatening these fragile cave systems, altering rainfall and groundwater patterns while destroying geological formations and underground ecosystems.
- As regulation remains limited, local communities are turning to carefully managed cave tourism and conservation to create livelihoods while protecting Meghalaya’s caves.
item.content:encoded: It’s an autumn morning at Mawmluh Cave, near Cherrapunji, in Meghalaya’s north-eastern hills. At the entrance, 27-year-old Milton Marak switches on his headlamp, and leads a group into the darkness. There are no electric lights inside. Only the beams from visitors’ torches illuminate towering stalagmites, delicate soda straws and curtains of calcite hanging from the cave ceiling. Marak was 18 when he first crawled into the Mawmluh Cave with nothing but a borrowed torch. Trained over two years, he knows the 7.2 kilometre cave well enough to navigate its passages without a map. “We’ve deliberately kept the cave natural,” he says. “If we install lights, it becomes a showroom. The real experience is entering a naturally dark cave with only your own light.” Marak adds that they could not rely on maps while guiding visitors. “We had to know every route by heart,” he says. Every visitor, while caving, is briefed to not touch the formations, litter, or carve their names into the cave walls. Only 25 people are allowed inside the Mawmluh cave each day. The rules, Marak says, exist for good reason. Mawmluh is more than a tourist attraction for people in Meghalaya and scientists worldwide. Beneath Meghalaya’s rain-soaked limestone hills, the caves hold a remarkable archive of the planet’s climate history, one that scientists now fear is increasingly vulnerable. Across Meghalaya’s limestone plateau, hundreds of such caves face growing pressure from two fronts: a changing climate is altering the rainfall and groundwater systems that shaped them over…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Kashmir musk deer face steep habitat losses under high emissions scenarios
item.dc:creator: Sneha Mahale
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Climate Change, Conservation, Endangered species, Extinction, Himalayas, Impacts of Climate Change, Mammals, and Protected Areas
item.description:
- A new study in the Kashmir Himalaya projects that climate change could sharply reduce suitable habitat for the endangered Kashmir musk deer. By 2071-2100, suitable habitat could decline by 82.6% under a very high-emissions scenario.
- Potential wildlife corridors could also contract by about half, making movement between protected areas more difficult and increasing the risk of population isolation.
- Most projected climate refugia lie outside protected areas, highlighting the need to protect high-elevation habitats, maintain connectivity and conserve key areas beyond reserve boundaries.
item.content:encoded: The Kashmir musk deer is a small, solitary, antlerless mountain species native to the western Himalaya, with a range extending across parts of Afghanistan, India and Pakistan. Unlike other deer, male Kashmir musk deer lack antlers, but possess elongated upper canines used primarily for territorial defence and competition for mates during the breeding season. Classified as ‘endangered’ on the IUCN Red List, the deer is threatened by poaching for its musk gland, habitat loss and fragmentation, and human disturbance. A new study in the Kashmir Himalaya finds that climate change could further reduce suitable habitat and weaken connectivity between remaining patches, potentially increasing the risk of population isolation. “The Kashmir musk deer is not controlled by climate alone. It is a forest-associated mountain species whose distribution is also shaped by elevation, ruggedness, forest structure and human disturbance,” says Mohsin Javid, from the Department of Wildlife Sciences at Aligarh Muslim University (AMU), and the corresponding author of the study. “The main gap was that habitat suitability and connectivity had rarely been assessed together for this species. We therefore asked not only where suitable habitat may persist under future climates, but whether those areas will remain connected enough to support dispersal, gene flow, recolonisation and climate-driven movement.” Kashmir musk deer play an important role as selective herbivores and prey within Himalayan ecosystems. They influence plant communities and contribute to nutrient cycling, while also serving as potential prey for predators such as leopards, shares Javid. “Conserving musk deer therefore means protecting not just…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Great Nicobar’s leatherbacks carry a unique genetic record that a megaport could bury
item.dc:creator: Madhusree Mukerjee
item.author: Simrinsirur
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Coast, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Environment, Evolution, Extinction, Habitat Loss, Indigenous Peoples, Industry, Islands, Oceans, and Wildlife
item.description:
- Leatherback turtles nested on the beaches of Galathea Bay, Great Nicobar Island, in record numbers last winter, new data show.
- These leatherbacks have relatively high genetic diversity, which increases the likelihood of a species surviving challenges such as climate change. It also underlines the necessity of protecting this leatherback population, experts say.
- No genetic research on Great Nicobar leatherbacks has been conducted since 2001, however, and is unlikely to be, given the Indian government’s plan to build a transshipment terminal at Galathea Bay.
item.content:encoded: Last winter, female leatherbacks heaved themselves onto a beach bordering Galathea Bay on Great Nicobar Island to dig and lay eggs in 869 nests, according to data from the Andaman and Nicobar Forest Department obtained through the Right to Information Act. That is the highest number of leatherback nests recorded on any beach in the Indian Ocean in this year’s nesting season, ending in March. In further good news, the numbers of leatherback nests not only on Galathea but also on the South Bay and West Bay beaches of Little Andaman Island have been going up in recent years, the data shows. Andaman and Nicobar is “the stronghold” of the Northeastern Indian Ocean leatherback population, said a researcher who did not wish to be named. “The population, being left alone, is thriving and likely overflowing” onto other beaches in the neighbourhood. “It’s common sense that Galathea is the epicentre of that nesting population,” says Hiltrud Cordes of the Turtle Foundation, which works with communities in Indonesia to protect marine turtles. That is, although leatherbacks in the Northeastern Indian Ocean also nest on other beaches of Andaman and Nicobar and on Sumatra, Galathea Bay in Great Nicobar Island shelters the most nests of all sites that have been consistently monitored. The new nesting data indicate that Galathea alone hosts about 175 or more leatherback mothers per year, more than estimated for all of Sumatra or the Andamans. Underscoring the significance of Galathea, the leatherbacks nesting there also have comparatively high genetic…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Early warning must also reach farmers without institutional support [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Vandana Choudhary and Milap Punia
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Climate Change, Climate Science, Drought, Extreme Weather Events, Food, and Impacts of Climate Change
item.description:
- Forecasts about this year’s El Nino and its impact on rain were known for some months but in Rajasthan, where drought is a recurring hazard, not all farmers received advisories based on weather.
- Farmers part of institutional networks such as local Krishi Vigyan Kendras (KVKs) do receive their advisories but precision and the scale of the forecast are challenges.
- For farmers outside such networks, lack of awareness about institutional support, messages delivered in technical and non-regional languages, and patchy network coverage, are all obstacles.
- The views, findings and analysis are those of the authors. The findings are not independently verified by Mongabay-India.
item.content:encoded: For India, an El Niño year has usually meant a weaker monsoon. That relationship is a tendency rather than a rule, and there have been El Niño years that ended with normal rain, but the odds move, and they move against us. This year the signal was unusually emphatic. The India Meteorological Department put the probability of El Niño developing during the monsoon season at 92%. The United States National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration gave it a 96% chance of persisting through the coming winter, and several analyses placed it in the ‘super El Niño territory’, comparable in strength to 2015. IMD’s seasonal outlook was for rainfall at 90% of the long period average, with a 60% likelihood that the season would close with a deficit. The monsoon followed the warning, and Rajasthan felt it early. By the first week of September, the state was 21% short of normal rainfall, with 21 of its districts deficient and only two in surplus. That put the state in step with a country that recorded a 13.8% shortfall between June and August, and where cumulative rainfall stayed about 15% below the long period average through September. Elsewhere the deficit has already turned into formal declarations, as in Maharashtra, which has declared drought in 265 of its 358 talukas. However, in the fields, the signal came earlier than any declaration. Nationally, kharif sowing lagged by about 16% on July 10, at 53.12 million hectares against 63.27 million a year earlier. item.title: ‘We cannot hold peace talks at gunpoint’: Security build-up deepens distrust over dam
item.dc:creator: Ranju Dodum
item.author: Simrinsirur
item.reporting-project: Hewing The Regulatory Tree and The India Water Story
item.topic-tags: Activism, Climate Change, Energy, and Rivers
item.description:
- Protests over the proposed Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) dam in Arunachal Pradesh have escalated into violence, arrests and a heavy security deployment.
- The state calls the dam a safeguard against China’s upstream hydropower project, while residents fear losing their land and the river.
- Protest groups say they will not meet the chief minister for negotiations until those detained are released.
item.content:encoded: On the morning of October 23, men and women sat outside the closed shops of Yingkiong’s main market in Upper Siang district, Arunachal Pradesh, talking about ordinary things, even though life in the Siang valley has been anything but. The market was deserted on account of a bandh, following weeks of unrest over the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP). Armed personnel in fatigues roamed the streets, and by the afternoon, the internet had been shut down in the entire district. “It feels as if they are deploying armed forces against us by force; like fighting an enemy on the border,” said Katin Burang, 44, a paddy and orange farmer from Gosang, a village near Yingkiong, who was at the market that day. “That is the change.” Hundreds of police personnel and paramilitary forces were deployed to the region since September 14, when residents called for a halt to all pre-feasibility studies (PFR) towards the SUMP – a massive hydroelectric and flood-control dam projected to generate roughly 11,200 MW of power. In early October, tensions escalated when four protesters were detained under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014. After a protest march demanding their release turned violent on October 23 – ending in damages to two MLAs’ homes and the office of the project developer, the NHPC, being set on fire – the crackdown intensified. The police has filed at least eight cases and arrested 26 people in connection to the violence. Search warrants were sought from the Chief…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: As wars reshape priorities, climate cooperation faces a test at the UN Climate Summit
item.dc:creator: Soumya Sarkar
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Clean Energy, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, and Climate Change Mitigation
item.description:
- As the UN climate summit starts in Türkiye’s Antalya, wars and energy insecurity are pulling governments towards short-term national interests although warming oceans, melting ice and accelerating climate impacts make collective action more urgent.
- Renewable energy offers a route to greater energy security, but the 35-by-35 pledge and Brazil’s fossil fuel exit roadmap to be discussed at the summit need firm national commitments and investment to deliver meaningful change.
- The annual climate conference has an ambitious agenda, but the prospects for significant progress are modest.
- Developing countries like India need substantially greater finance and support to adapt to climate damage and pursue a just transition.
item.content:encoded: When delegates from around the world gather in the Mediterranean resort town of Antalya in the Turkish Riviera for the annual, two-week United Nations climate summit (COP31) that begins on November 9, they meet at a time when wars and geopolitical rivalries are pushing governments to protect their immediate national interests even as rising temperatures, warming oceans and melting ice are making the costs of delayed climate action harder to contain. Although the need for countries to work together has rarely been greater, their willingness to do so is far less certain. The formal negotiations at the UN climate conference in Antalya will address adaptation and resilience, emissions reduction, climate finance and a just transition. Alongside them, the Turkish host’s action agenda will pursue practical progress on clean energy, electrification, food security, oceans and resilient cities, bringing together businesses, investors and other groups. Türkiye’s 35-by-35 electrification pledge and previous host Brazil’s roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels offer grounds for progress. Renewable energy continues to expand despite political and economic uncertainty. But the gap between the climate crisis and the political response remains enormous. COP31 could advance the work, but it is unlikely to resolve the contradictions that hold it back. A planet under pressure The evidence is stark. The World Meteorological Organization’s State of the Global Climate 2025 confirms that 2015-25 were the 11 hottest years on record. The planet’s energy imbalance has reached its highest level in 65 years, while oceans have absorbed enormous amounts of excess…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Two losses this year, but authorities say great Indian bustard’s rewilding is on track
item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Birds, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Extinction, Grasslands, National Parks, Protected Areas, and Wildlife
item.description:
- India has begun releasing captive-bred Great Indian Bustards into the wild as part of its bid to revive the critically-endangered bird, but one of the first four birds released in Rajasthan was predated within days.
- Although the captive-breeding programme has reported high survival rates, post-release survival is expected to be much lower, with scientists estimating it at around 30%.
- Questions are also being raised over the programme’s preparedness and transparency, particularly its approach to predator management in the Great Indian Bustard’s habitat.
item.content:encoded: In what is being considered a milestone for Project Great Indian Bustard, four captive-bred great Indian bustards (GIBs) were released into the wild in early October at the Desert National Park in Rajasthan. On October 17, one of the four birds was found dead, apparently predated upon by a desert fox the day before. The authorities, however, do not consider the loss a setback. Sutirtha Dutta, a lead scientist with the Wildlife Institute of India (WII), informs Mongabay-India that mortality due to predation and starvation, as well as threats posed by existing infrastructure, is expected during rewilding. Earlier this year, a GIB chick hatched in the wild in Kutch, Gujarat, in March after a fertilised egg was transported from the conservation breeding centre at Sam in Rajasthan’s Jaisalmer. It then went missing in April and could not be traced despite searches by forest officials. The egg had been transported as part of the Jumpstart Approach, an attempt to restore a breeding population of GIBs in Gujarat, another former range state of the bird. The approach uses eggs from Rajasthan’s captive-breeding programme and gets wild female bustards in Gujarat to incubate and rear the chicks. Forest department officials suspected that the chick had been predated upon, although no remains were recovered. Its disappearance prompted the state government to strengthen habitat protection, fencing and predator-management measures. A desert fox. item.content:encoded: The Bombay Natural History Society (BNHS) recently published, in collaboration with Harper Collins Publishers India, a book titled Mammals of India. The book is authored by two well-respected wildlife researchers — A.J.T. Johnsingh and P.O. Nameer. Johnsingh died in 2024, before he could see the book through to its publication. Mongabay-India spoke with Nameer, Dean at the College of Forestry at the Kerala Agrucultural University in Thrissur. In the conversation, Nameer recalls how the project on compiling a book on India’s mammalian biodiversity started in 2018. The idea was to publish a book that is equally of importance to the wildlife researchers and non-expert readers. India has a unique heritage of mammalian diversity, considering its geological and biogeographic history. Having broken off from the African landmass and drifted through the sea through millions of years, it collided with the Eurasian landmass around 50 million years ago. The Himalayas rose at the point of collision, folding and thrusting upwards as the Indian and Eurasian landmass moved closer to each other. However, this process of joining happened staggered over millions of years, leading to multiple stages of connections and disconnections for the spread of mammals. The world’s highest ridge — the Himalayas — resulted in change in the monsoon system, which is the annual movement and retreat of moisture-laden winds from the sea to the land. item.title: A native tarantula as a seasonal food
item.dc:creator: Sabir Nishat
item.author: Divya Kilikar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Ecology, Endemic species, Food, Forests, Indigenous Peoples, Natural Resources, Sustainability, Tribes, Villages, and Wildlife
item.description:
- A new study documents the traditional consumption of the Indian black earth tiger spider, collected by the Rabha community from sal forests in Assam.
- While agriculture is practised by a majority of Rabhas, fishing, weaving, livestock rearing and the collection of forest resources are also integral to their livelihoods. The traditional consumption of the spider is a longstanding cultural practice that has been passed over generations.
- Systematic studies on the consumption of arachnids remains limited in India and beyond, with little knowledge on populations, nutrient composition and ecology.
item.content:encoded: In the forest-fringe villages of Kamrup (rural) district, Assam, the emergence of a large, endemic tarantula signals the arrival of a seasonal food for the Rabha community. The Rabhas, also known as Ravas, are an Indigenous community that predominantly reside in Goalpara and Kamrup districts in western Assam, along with smaller settlements in other parts of Assam, Meghalaya and West Bengal. A new study published in Proceedings of the Zoological Society documents the community’s consumption of the Indian black earth tiger spider (Lyrognathus crotalus). Locally known as bhaluk makara, it is collected from April to June every year, when they are observed by the Rabhas to be most abundant. Researchers Jyotiprakash Boro, Kuldeep Bora, Chandramita Boro and Samir Terdalkar conducted fieldwork between April and June 2025, interviewing 34 community members in and around Mouman village, including elders and spider collectors. Collecting spiders for a diverse diet The spiders are collected during three to four days a month during the pre-monsoon months and occasionally at other times of the year, depending on availability. A collection trip can yield about 20 to 30 spiders. The Indian black earth tiger spider is collected and consumed by the Rabha community during the pre-monsoon months, when they are considered abundant. Image by Prasanna Bonyabondhu. Collectors locate the spiders by finding their burrows in near forests, particularly those associated with sal (Shorea robusta) trees. A new study examines how artificial light at night (ALAN), including the diffuse glow produced when artificial light scatters in the atmosphere, affects […]
item.content:encoded: In protected areas, artificial light at night can affect wildlife in several ways, potentially changing where animals live and move, how they navigate, their reproductive behaviour and interactions between predators and prey. A new study examines how artificial light at night (ALAN), including the diffuse glow produced when artificial light scatters in the atmosphere, affects the night-time environments of protected areas in Kerala’s Western Ghats. The study not only investigates illumination within protected areas but also how surrounding human settlements, roads, places of worship, tourism facilities and other activity centres may contribute to light pollution. The researchers assessed 21 protected areas, using satellite-derived night-time light data from 2024 and infrastructure information from OpenStreetMap. The study mentions that these protected areas are close to human habitation, exposing them to ALAN. They examined light exposure within protected areas and in five surrounding distance zones: 0-2 km, 2-5 km, 5-10 km, 10-20 km and 20-30 km. Light levels varied considerably between reserves studied, with Periyar Tiger Reserve West recording the highest average and maximum light levels measured by satellite data. One of the main takeaways is that within protected areas, the density of places of worship was most strongly associated with light levels. “We found ALAN to be closely related to places of worship with high levels of artificial light and illumination at night,” informs Haripriya S., the lead author of the study. item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. Decades after disappearing from Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh, the gaur or Indian bison made a comeback following conservation efforts, according to media reports. In 2011-12, a herd of 40 gaur were reintroduced from Kanha Tiger Reserve, and today, Bandhavgarh’s gaur population stands at over 220. The gaur (Bos gaurus) is the world’s largest wild bovine. Bulls can grow up to two metres in height, and weigh about 1,500 kg — as much as a car! Males have dark, almost black coats, while females are a lighter reddish-brown. Both have upward-curving horns and a shoulder hump, most prominent in adult males. Despite their size, gaur are shy animals, living in small herds often led by a matriarch. They graze and browse on grasses, bamboo, and leaves, thus dispersing seeds, tilling the soil and maintaining ecosystem balance. They are also prey for animals like tigers, leopards, and the dholes. Gaur inhabit evergreen and deciduous forests across the Western Ghats and central and northeastern India, and are the state animals of Goa and Bihar. They also occur in Nepal, Bhutan, China and parts of Southeast Asia. Their estimated global population is between 13,000 and 30,000, with about 85% in India. The International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Species categorises the gaur as ‘vulnerable’. In India, it receives the highest legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972. item.title: El Niño link offers early warning of humid heat
item.dc:creator: Archita Bhatta
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Climate Change, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Global Warming, Health impacts, Human Rights, and Impacts of Climate Change
item.description:
- With El Niño emerging as a major concern this year, a study finds a strong link between ENSO and year-to-year variations in productivity losses from humid heat stress.
- The study highlights the increasing frequency of humid heat stress. However, it also finds that ENSO-linked humid heat stress and productivity losses can be predicted up to six months in advance, allowing time for preparation.
- Experts call for better forecasting of humid heat stress and productivity losses, along with measures such as changing outdoor working hours and providing shelters for vulnerable people.
item.content:encoded: Manoj Borah is a welfare officer at a tea garden in Kamrup district in Assam. He says working outdoors in tea gardens and agricultural fields is becoming increasingly difficult. “While workers are used to daytime heat, the high temperature during the night is burning them out. It is difficult to rest at night, and this is taking a toll on their health. Without proper rest, it is difficult to go out and work in the fields the next day. In the last few years, we have had to shift the outdoor working hours so that they start at 5 AM and do not have to stretch beyond noon,” he said. India accounts for more than half of the global rise in potential productivity loss from extreme humid heat since the mid-1980s, according to a new study published in Journal of Geophysical Research (JGR) Atmospheres, a journal of the American Geophysical Union. “Outdoor workers in agriculture or industry, as well as those involved in exercise and sports, are advised to stop their vocation during extreme humid heat, as continued exposure can lead to severe medical conditions like heat stroke and even death,” said Subodh Kumar Saha, a scientist at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (IITM), Pune and also the paper’s corresponding author. The study also offers some hope. Humid heat stress is closely linked to the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO), a natural cycle of warming and cooling in the tropical Pacific Ocean that shifts weather patterns worldwide.
